prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I still place the optical lattice clock first. Katori's magic-wavelength idea is simple enough to explain with one picture: atoms held in light that does not shift the transition being counted. Ye's group then drove the platform to record stability and accuracy and linked it to the frequency comb. Many independent laboratories on several continents now reproduce and surpass each other, and the clocks are checked directly against one another, which is the kind of robust, cross-checked precision I trust. The work has opened new questions, such as millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, constraints on varying constants and dark-matter searches, and it was unexpected that neutral atoms in a lattice could beat ion clocks. The prize would reward a fundamental advance in measurement, not a technological product, though the redefinition of the second will follow. A two-person configuration is clean.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the field is a continuation of ground already honoured: frequency combs in 2005 and ion-clock quantum control in 2012. Some will see the lattice clock as an incremental, instrument-led step rather than a discovery of something new in nature. The credit boundary is also not airtight, since the Paris, JILA, PTB and RIKEN groups all made decisive contributions, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. I also have to note that atomic and precision physics is my home field, so I should guard against favouring it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as the clearest case of a measurement technique opening new science, with a clean Katori and Ye pairing and well-documented systematics.
responses.response: I agree with the pairing and with the weight he gives to measured systematics and independent reproduction. I would add that the argument for a prize is not only that the clocks are precise but that agreement between independent clocks at 10^-18 turns precision into a test of physics. I also share his caution that the redefinition of the second is pending, and I would not make that a requirement; the scientific case stands on the comparisons already made. Where I differ slightly is that I would not call this a technique with an application milestone still to come; the physics results are already in hand.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first because Bistritzer and MacDonald's flat-band prediction was followed by the correlated and superconducting phases found by Jarillo-Herrero's group, a prediction-then-experiment loop.
responses.response: I agree that this loop is the pattern I value, and I accept that many groups reproduce the correlated phases. My reservation is about whether the physics is understood. The origin of the superconductivity is still debated and the samples depend strongly on twist-angle disorder, so I am not yet convinced that a prize would honour a settled picture, as opposed to a very exciting open one. I also think Andrei's early flat-band evidence makes the allocation to three people less clean than he suggests. If the committee wants a condensed matter prize this year I can accept B014, but I would want to hear from the condensed matter members how secure the interpretation really is.

responses.point: Danielsson puts IceCube and Halzen first as a clear discovery from nature, an observation that opens neutrino astronomy, and accepts that a single name stands in for a collaboration.
responses.response: I defer to him on astroparticle physics and I agree that observation of something new is exactly what the prize should reward. Pearce's concern about AMANDA and the collaboration makes a one-person prize hard for me to accept as fairly attributed, and the source of most of the diffuse flux is still unexplained. I would like to know from him whether other names should be credited before I could support B016 over the clock. I did not put it on my own list, which reflects my lack of expertise rather than any judgement on its merit.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the discovery of a strong-coupling regime, while noting that the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits makes timing a concern.
responses.response: I take his point that circuit QED is a real discovery of a regime and not only a technology. But I share his worry about proximity to the 2025 prize, and I think the same argument about overlap with prior prizes applies to my own clock candidate, so I should not apply it only to his. I would still put the clock ahead for now because the clock's scientific payoff, in precision tests, is further from the 2012 and 2025 territory than circuit QED is from 2025.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as disqualifying or as irrelevant for the lattice clock.
Whether the credit should be limited to Katori and Ye or should include a third name from the Paris, PTB or JILA groups; I cannot settle this from the supplied credit list.
Whether the unresolved mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene weakens its case enough to put it behind the clock.
Who among the credited ultracold-atom names would be a fair three-person selection for B031.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B013, B014, B041, B003, B021 or B016. I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate, and have co-authored with the Lund group and with Ursula Keller's group, but none of them is a credited name on the shortlisted candidates. I work in atomic physics, which is close to B013, B031 and B017, so I note it as a possible source of bias rather than a recusal issue.
